results.content:
## Publication and experimental evidence

| Requested item | Information explicitly stated on the page |
|---|---|
| **Title** | “CRISPR screens unveil signal hubs for nutrient licensing of T cell immunity” |
| **CRISPR perturbation modality** | The study used **genome-wide CRISPR screening**, combined with protein–protein interaction networks, to identify regulatory modules involved in immune receptor- and nutrient-dependent signaling to mTORC1. The page does **not** specify the CRISPR system or state that the genome-wide screen used knockout perturbations exclusively. It separately reports “loss of SEC31A” and “specific deletion of Ccdc101” in mouse Treg cells. |
| **Perturbed cell compartment** | **Mouse regulatory T (Treg) cells**. The abstract describes screening for signaling in mouse Treg cells and reports SEC31A loss and specific Ccdc101 deletion in mouse Treg cells. |
| **Immune context** | Nutrient and immune-receptor signals regulating mTORC1; T-cell priming; Treg suppressive function and immune tolerance; uncontrolled inflammation and improved antitumour immunity following Ccdc101 deletion in mouse Treg cells. |
| **Readouts and reported effects** | mTORC1 activation/activity; protection of GATOR2 component SEC13 from SKP1-dependent proteasomal degradation through interaction with SEC31A; T-cell priming; Treg suppressive function; expression of amino-acid sensor CASTOR1; expression of glucose and amino-acid transporters; T-cell quiescence in vivo; inflammation; and antitumour immunity. The page does not specify a single assay or provide quantitative readout values. |
| **Biological model** | **Mouse** Treg cells and mice. The abstract states that SEC31A loss impairs T-cell priming and Treg suppressive function “in mice,” and that specific Ccdc101 deletion in mouse Treg cells results in uncontrolled inflammation and improved antitumour immunity. |

## Possible effects of the specified restrictions

| Restriction | What it could exclude, based on the page | Evidence versus inference |
|---|---|---|
| **Cancer-cell-only** | Could exclude this study’s described perturbations and main cellular focus, which are in T cells—specifically mouse Treg cells—rather than cancer cells. | The Treg focus is explicit. The page mentions improved **antitumour immunity**, but does not say that cancer cells were the perturbed compartment. |
| **CRISPR-knockout-only** | Could exclude the genome-wide screen if eligibility requires an explicitly documented knockout modality: the page identifies genome-wide CRISPR screening but does not specify that the screen was knockout-only. | The screening modality is explicit; knockout-only screening is **not**. The page separately reports SEC31A loss and specific Ccdc101 deletion, but does not establish that every screening perturbation was a knockout. |
| **Co-culture-only** | Could exclude the reported in-vivo mouse/Treg evidence if eligibility requires co-culture experiments. | In-vivo mouse findings are explicit. The page does **not** report co-culture experiments; their presence or absence cannot be established beyond the supplied page content. |
| **RNA-seq-only** | Could exclude the study if eligibility requires RNA-seq as the experimental modality or readout: the page describes genome-wide CRISPR screening and protein–protein interaction networks, not RNA-seq. | CRISPR screening and protein–protein interaction networks are explicit. RNA-seq is **not stated**; the page does not establish whether it was used elsewhere in the study. |

results.title: CRISPR activation and interference screens decode stimulation ...
results.content:
| Requested information | Explicit evidence on the page |
|---|---|
| Publication title | **CRISPR activation and interference screens decode stimulation responses in primary human T cells** |
| CRISPR perturbation modality | The abstract reports **genome-wide CRISPR activation (CRISPRa)** and **CRISPR interference (CRISPRi)** screens. It also reports **arrayed CRISPRa** to confirm key hits and characterize the secretome. No CRISPR knockout screen is stated. |
| Perturbed cell compartment | **Primary human T cells**. The page does not specify a T-cell subset. |
| Immune context | **Stimulated T cells**; the study investigates stimulation-dependent regulation of cytokine production. The abstract identifies interleukin-2 (**IL-2**) and interferon-γ (**IFN-γ**) as cytokine targets. The specific stimulation method is not stated. |
| Readouts | **IL-2 and IFN-γ production**; multiplexed **secretome characterization** following arrayed CRISPRa; and **single-cell RNA sequencing** coupled with CRISPRa screening to characterize screen hits and cell states. |
| Biological model | Genome-wide CRISPRa and CRISPRi screens in **primary human T cells**. |

| Restriction | What it could exclude, based on the page |
|---|---|
| Cancer-cell-only | **Could exclude this study** under a cancer-cell-only model requirement: the stated experimental model is primary human T cells, not cancer cells. The page mentions cancer as motivation and immunotherapies as a possible application, but does not state that cancer cells were experimentally perturbed. |
| CRISPR-knockout-only | **Could exclude this study** under a knockout-only modality requirement: the stated modalities are CRISPRa and CRISPRi. CRISPRi is described as interference, not as knockout, and no CRISPR knockout screen is reported. |
| Co-culture-only | **Could exclude this study if co-culture is required**, because the page does not report a co-culture experiment. It identifies primary human T cells, but does not specify whether cultures included other cell types. |
| RNA-seq-only | **Could exclude this study** under an RNA-seq-only readout requirement: single-cell RNA sequencing is reported, but so are cytokine-production measurements and multiplexed secretome characterization. |

**Evidence boundary:** The listed cell type, perturbation modalities, stimulation context, cytokines, and readouts are explicitly stated in the abstract. Any eligibility decision under the restrictions above is an inference from those statements; the page does not explicitly classify the study against such restrictions.
results.description: Regulation of cytokine production in stimulated T cells can be disrupted in autoimmunity, immunodeficiencies, and cancer. Systematic discovery of stimulation-dependent cytokine regulators requires both loss-of-function and gain-of-function studies, which have been challenging in primary human cells. …
